newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl sees compromise chances in coal talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl sees compromise chances in coal talks.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Wednesday he saw good chances of reaching an agreement over planned cuts in coal subsidies in a meeting with German mining union leader Hans Berger on Thursday.
Kohl told journalists in Munich he favoured a step-by-step approach that would help ease the effect of the deep cuts he wants to make in subsidies for the industry by the year 2005.

Industry sources said mining company Ruhrkohle and utility Veba had put forward a new plan suggesting the government raise its offer by an annual 650 million marks ($380.6 million) until 2000 to stave off the closure of several mines.

Unions say Bonn's current plan would mean the end of between five and seven pits in the next three years as subsidies are ended immediately for domestic coal provided to the steel industry, creating 10 million tonnes of excess capacity.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) also made more conciliatory noises, saying for the first time they would not continue boycotting tax reform talks with the government even if Kohl failed to make a satisfactory offer to the pit workers.
"I want the coal industry to survive and experts say that's possible at a lower level (than today)," Kohl said. "But we have to go step-by-step (with the cuts) between now and 2005."
Speaking after meeting business leaders at a trade fair, Kohl said he was optimistic the two sides could reach an agreement "with a bit of goodwill".

Sources close to Kohl's coalition said the government was considering improving welfare benefits for miners in the next three years to ease the pain of the cuts, but said it would not drop its goal of cutting subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005.

The free-market Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners, said they were prepared to hold their ground against the massive protests but hinted they could be more flexible on the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.

FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms, whose party as the driving force behind the proposed cuts, has been locked out of its own headquarters in Bonn by the miners, said the FDP did not want shock measures and sudden mine closures.
The opposition SPD, who rule the two main mining states, have strongly backed the miners and said tempers would flare if the government could not come up with concessions on Thursday.
"Then the situation will become critical," said SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine, premier of the coal-producing Saar state, in a firebreathing speech at a rally in Bonn.
Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the 6.5 billion marks the unions want.
Bonn argues it can no longer afford to pay over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.

Thousands of miners paralysed Bonn's government district for three days running but began leaving on Wednesday so that Kohl, who called off a meeting with Berger on Tuesday because of the threat of violence, would come back to the table on Thursday. ($ = 1.708 German Marks)
